about: Reference recordings of wild eastern screech-owl (Megascops asio), all from xeno-canto, all from the United States (Pennsylvania, Delaware, Colorado, Massachusetts, Florida, Tennessee, Wisconsin, Alabama). Licenses and the 'Playback used' field were checked on each recording's own page on 2026-11-13; every recording used says 'Playback used: no'. Pages describing a response to playback or to a whistled imitation were skipped even when 'Playback used' was 'no' (e.g. XC820866, XC336371, XC368483, XC301668), as were recordings the recordist filtered or noise-reduced (e.g. XC544849, XC624995, XC669305, XC1087470, XC310034, XC1071056), and southern Texas and Mexico (McCall's screech-owl, which Birds of the World says never gives the whinny). trimStartSec/trimEndSec are seconds in the original file as downloaded. Each clip keeps about 0.45 s before the call for the noise floor. Calls were classified by measurement against the cited definitions in callDefinitions; uncertain clips say so (uncertain: true).

callDefinitions.readVia: shortcut: all sources were read through web-search excerpts and search summaries, because this build environment's network blocks allaboutbirds.org, birdsoftheworld.org, mdc.mo.gov and dnr.state.mn.us (checked 2026-11-13). The quotes below are from those excerpts; where only a search summary was available the text says so. Re-read the pages directly when next editing the app text.

calls.name: Monotone trill
calls.definition: 'Their most common sounds are an even-pitched trill, often called a "bounce song" or tremolo; and a shrill, descending whinny' (All About Birds). The trill is mostly given at a single pitch but may rise or fall slightly at the end (Birds of the World, search excerpt). Missouri Department of Conservation: 'Most often heard is the screech-owl's trilling (an even-pitched sound referred to as a tremolo)'. Minnesota DNR: a monotone trill on a single pitch.
calls.use: 'The tremolo is used by pairs or families to keep in touch and is 3-6 seconds long' (All About Birds). Male and female give both the trill and the whinny (Minnesota DNR, search summary).
calls.classifyBy: one continuous run of even pulses held at one pitch (start, middle and end within about 50 Hz). Measured here: 2.1-5.7 s, about 10-17 pulses per second (10 ms autocorrelation steps, coarse), 560-818 Hz.
calls.caveat: Several clips (2.1-2.6 s) are shorter than All About Birds' 3-6 s; a Birds of the World search excerpt says a typical trill in Kentucky averaged about 2.3 s, so length is not used to classify.

calls.name: Descending whinny
calls.definition: 'A shrill, descending whinny' (All About Birds). Birds of the World (search excerpt): 'Typically, the initial portion exhibits a slight increase in frequency, and the latter portion a gradual decrease in frequency.' Missouri Department of Conservation: 'a call that sounds like a descending whinny'.
calls.use: Territorial defense (All About Birds and Birds of the World, via a search summary: about 0.5-2 s, used to defend territories). Birds of the World (search excerpt): in territorial adults it is elicited particularly by dispersing juveniles.
calls.classifyBy: one call that falls in pitch from its first fifth to its last fifth, 0.5-2 s long. Measured here: 0.9-1.4 s, from 883-1238 Hz in the first fifth down to 754-1012 Hz in the last fifth.
calls.caveat: Birds of the World (search excerpt): the McCall's form of southern Texas and northern Mexico never gives the whinny; no clip comes from that range.

notIncluded: Screech, hoots, barks: Birds of the World / All About Birds (search excerpts) describe screeches as loud, piercing or grating calls of agitated owls defending nests or fledglings, and hoots as milder alarm. Only a few allowed recordings are labelled as alarm calls or barks (XC433677, XC569789, XC771182), with no description detailed enough to classify them against. Not included rather than guessed.
Wail, squeal, bill snapping and juvenile calls (XC771179, XC771180, XC771181, XC786184, XC563930, XC573237, XC661912): no cited description found to classify against.
Duet: Missouri Department of Conservation says the trill and whinny are sometimes given as a duet between mates. Two birds; not cut per bird.
